title: Get set up
text: You need two things: R, which does the calculations, and a place to type and run it. Choose one of the two options below.

title: Get set up
text:
Option A: in your browser (recommended)
Nothing to install, and it works on any laptop with a web browser.

Go to posit.cloud and create a free account.
Click New Project, then New RStudio Project.
In the panel called Console, paste this line and press Enter. It installs the packages the workshop uses, and takes a few minutes the first time:

install.packages(c("readxl", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "epifitter", "lme4"))

Download the two data files from Data and credits and upload them using the Upload button in the Files panel. Put them in a folder called data.

title: Get set up
section: Option B: on your own computer
text:
Option B: on your own computer

Install R from cran.r-project.org.
Install RStudio Desktop (free) from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop.
Open RStudio and run the same install.packages(...) line as in Option A.
Make a folder for the workshop with a data folder inside it, and save the two data files there.

title: Get set up
text:
Check that it works
Paste this into the console. If it prints the number of fields in the survey, you are ready.
library(readxl)
field <- read_excel("data/cassava_mosaic_survey.xlsx", sheet = "Field")
nrow(field)
It should print 512.

title: Get set up
text:
If you get stuck
Do not worry if something does not install the first time; it happens to everyone. Copy the exact error message into a search engine, which solves most problems. If you are still stuck, open an issue on GitHub and paste the message there.

title: 1. Reading disease data
text:
Cassava mosaic disease is caused by viruses that turn cassava leaves into a yellow-green patchwork and stunt the plant. It reaches a field in two ways:

in the planting material, when farmers plant stem cuttings taken from infected plants, or
by whiteflies, which carry the virus from plant to plant as they feed.

In 2015 and 2017, researchers from the Central and West African Virus Epidemiology (WAVE) programme’s hub at Covenant University walked 512 cassava fields across 13 states in South-West and North-Central Nigeria and recorded what they saw. Their data are free for anyone to use. Today we use them to answer two questions: how much disease was there, and where did it come from?

title: 1. Reading disease data
text:
Cassava mosaic disease is caused by viruses that turn cassava leaves into a yellow-green patchwork and stunt the plant. It reaches a field in two ways:

in the planting material, when farmers plant stem cuttings taken from infected plants, or
by whiteflies, which carry the virus from plant to plant as they feed.

In 2015 and 2017, researchers from the Central and West African Virus Epidemiology (WAVE) programme’s hub at Covenant University walked 512 cassava fields across 13 states in South-West and North-Central Nigeria and recorded what they saw. Their data are free for anyone to use. Today we use them to answer two questions: how much disease was there, and where did it come from?

title: 1. Reading disease data
text:
First steps in R (15 minutes)
If you have never used R, start here. Type each line into the console and press Enter.
R is a calculator:

2 + 3

[1] 5


You can store a result under a name with <-, and use the name later:

plants <- 100
diseased <- 40
diseased / plants

[1] 0.4


A function does a job. You give it something in brackets, and it gives an answer back:

heights <- c(12, 15, 9, 20)   # c() combines numbers into a list
mean(heights)

[1] 14

max(heights)

[1] 20


A table of data is called a data frame. Each row is one thing (here, one field) and each column is one measurement. You will meet one in a moment.
Packages add extra tools. You install them once (see Get set up), and switch them on each time you start R with library().
That is all you need for today.

title: 1. Reading disease data
text:
Load the data

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

field <- read_excel("data/cassava_mosaic_survey.xlsx", sheet = "Field")
nrow(field)

[1] 512

names(field)

 [1] "Year"               "Field"              "Country"           
 [4] "State"              "Altitude"           "Mean_CMD_Severity" 
 [7] "CMD_Incidence"      "Cutting_Infection"  "Whitefly_Infection"
[10] "Total_whitefly"    


Each row is one field. The columns we need:







Column
What it means




Year
2015 or 2017


State
the state the field is in


CMD_Incidence
the share of plants in the field showing symptoms, from 0 to 1


Mean_CMD_Severity
how bad the symptoms were, on a 1 to 5 scale, averaged over the diseased plants


Cutting_Infection
the share of the infection that came in with the planting material


Whitefly_Infection
the share that was carried in by whiteflies


Total_whitefly
how many whiteflies were counted in the field

title: 1. Reading disease data
section: Incidence and severity are different things
text:
Incidence and severity are different things
These two words get mixed up all the time, so it is worth being precise:

Incidence asks how many plants are diseased. A field with 40 sick plants out of 100 has an incidence of 0.4.
Severity asks how badly a plant is affected. A plant can be diseased but only mildly.

A field can have high incidence and low severity (many plants, mild symptoms), or the reverse. You need both to describe an outbreak.
Cassava mosaic severity is scored on a 1 to 5 scale, from 1 (no symptoms) to 5 (severe mosaic, distorted leaves and a stunted plant). The numbers are ordered categories, not measurements: a score of 4 is worse than a 2, but it is not “twice as bad”. Keep that in mind whenever you average scores like these.

title: 1. Reading disease data
text:
How much disease was there?

field |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(
    fields         = n(),
    mean_incidence = mean(CMD_Incidence),
    mean_severity  = mean(Mean_CMD_Severity, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 4
   Year fields mean_incidence mean_severity
  <dbl>  <int>          <dbl>         <dbl>
1  2015    184          0.438          2.73
2  2017    328          0.122          2.15


In 2015, on average 44% of plants in a field showed symptoms. By 2017 that had fallen to about 12%.
A picture shows the spread across fields, not just the average:

ggplot(field, aes(x = factor(Year), y = CMD_Incidence)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#d8e9d0") +
  labs(x = "Survey year", y = "Share of plants with symptoms",
       title = "Cassava mosaic incidence in 512 Nigerian fields") +
  theme_minimal()

title: 1. Reading disease data
section: Where did the infection come from?
text:
Where did the infection come from?
The route of infection is only recorded for fields that had some disease, so we keep just those:

diseased <- field |> filter(CMD_Incidence > 0)
nrow(diseased)

[1] 360

summary(diseased$Cutting_Infection)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0000  0.7088  0.9091  0.8070  1.0000  1.0000 


The median field got about 91% of its infection from the planting material. Let us count how many fields got at least half of it that way, and how many got more than half:

diseased |>
  summarise(
    fields              = n(),
    at_least_half       = mean(Cutting_Infection >= 0.5),
    more_than_half      = mean(Cutting_Infection > 0.5)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fields at_least_half more_than_half
   <int>         <dbl>          <dbl>
1    360           0.9           0.85


In nine out of ten diseased fields, at least half of the disease was planted, not caught, and in 85% it was more than half. Notice how much the wording matters: “at least half” and “more than half” give different numbers, because 18 fields sit at exactly 50%. That changes what a farmer should do: the first defence is clean planting material, not spraying for whiteflies.

title: 1. Reading disease data
text:
Your turn






NoteExercise 1



Which state had the highest average incidence in 2017?








TipAnswer






field |>
  filter(Year == 2017) |>
  group_by(State) |>
  summarise(mean_incidence = mean(CMD_Incidence), fields = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_incidence))

# A tibble: 13 × 3
   State     mean_incidence fields
   <chr>              <dbl>  <int>
 1 Benue             0.264      34
 2 Lagos             0.207       9
 3 Niger             0.2        13
 4 Ogun              0.181      36
 5 FCT               0.167       2
 6 Nassarawa         0.119      30
 7 Ekiti             0.103      20
 8 Oyo               0.0913     50
 9 Ondo              0.0846     39
10 Kwara             0.0817     20
11 Kogi              0.0667     32
12 Plateau           0.0606     11
13 Osun              0.0604     32


Check the fields column too: an average from three fields is much less reliable than one from fifty.









NoteExercise 2



Do fields with more whiteflies get more of their infection from whiteflies? Make a plot of Total_whitefly against Whitefly_Infection for the diseased fields.








TipAnswer






ggplot(diseased, aes(x = Total_whitefly + 1, y = Whitefly_Infection)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Whiteflies counted (+1, log scale)",
       y = "Share of infection from whiteflies") +
  theme_minimal()







cor(diseased$Total_whitefly, diseased$Whitefly_Infection, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.2969913


There is a link, but a loose one. The whitefly count is one visit on one day, while the symptoms record the whole season. A single count is a snapshot of something that keeps changing.

title: 1. Reading disease data
text:
What to take away

Always ask how many (incidence) and how badly (severity) separately.
Treat 1 to 5 scores as ordered categories, not measurements.
A survey can tell you not only how much disease there is, but where it came from, and that decides what farmers should do about it.

title: 2. How epidemics grow
text:
Picture a field of 100 leaves where one is infected. Spores from that one leaf land on the 99 healthy ones, so new infections appear slowly at first. As more leaves become infected, there are more sources of spores and the epidemic speeds up. But later there are few healthy leaves left to infect, so it slows down again.
So the speed of an epidemic depends on two things multiplied together:

how much disease there is to spread from (call it \(y\)), and
how much healthy tissue is left to spread to (\(1 - y\)).




Diseased share \(y\)
Healthy share \(1-y\)
Sources times targets




0.01
0.99
0.0099 (slow)


0.50
0.50
0.25 (fastest)


0.99
0.01
0.0099 (slow again)



Slow, then fast, then slow is the S-shaped curve. It is called the logistic model, and its formula is:
\[
y(t) = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{1 - y_0}{y_0}\, e^{-r t}}
\]
where \(y_0\) is the share diseased at the start and \(r\) is how fast the epidemic grows.

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

logistic <- function(t, y0, r) 1 / (1 + ((1 - y0) / y0) * exp(-r * t))

curve_data <- tibble(t = 0:40) |>
  mutate(slow = logistic(t, 0.01, 0.15),
         fast = logistic(t, 0.01, 0.30))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = slow, colour = "r = 0.15")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fast, colour = "r = 0.30")) +
  labs(x = "Days", y = "Share diseased", colour = NULL,
       title = "Two logistic epidemics starting from 1% disease") +
  theme_minimal()

title: 2. How epidemics grow
section: The one test every model must pass
text:
The one test every model must pass
Here is a simple check that catches a surprising number of mistakes, including errors that get printed in textbooks. Put \(t = 0\) into the formula. The answer must be \(y_0\), the starting level, because that is what \(y_0\) means.
Below are two versions of the logistic formula. One is correct. The other was once printed in an open epidemiology textbook, before a reader reported the error and it was corrected:

correct <- function(t, y0, r) 1 / (1 + ((1 - y0) / y0) * exp(-r * t))
printed <- function(t, y0, r) 1 / (1 + (1 - y0) * exp(-r * t))

correct(t = 0, y0 = 0.01, r = 0.3)

[1] 0.01

printed(t = 0, y0 = 0.01, r = 0.3)

[1] 0.5025126


The correct version gives 0.01, which is what we started with. The printed one gives 0.50, claiming the field was already half diseased on day zero. Now look at day 15:

correct(t = 15, y0 = 0.01, r = 0.3)

[1] 0.476238

printed(t = 15, y0 = 0.01, r = 0.3)

[1] 0.9891217


The printed formula says the crop is about 99% diseased when the truth is under half. A student who trusted it might give up on a field that could still be saved. One line of arithmetic, checking \(t = 0\), would have caught it.

title: 2. How epidemics grow
text:
A real epidemic
Now look at real data. The epifitter package comes with measurements of powdery mildew on tomato, taken every week:

library(epifitter)

mildew <- PowderyMildew |>
  filter(irrigation_type == "Drip", moisture == "High moisture") |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(sev = mean(sev))

ggplot(mildew, aes(time, sev)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Days", y = "Share of leaf diseased",
       title = "Powdery mildew on tomato") +
  theme_minimal()








You can see the epidemic building through the season. Fitting a curve to points like these gives you the growth rate \(r\), so you can compare epidemics fairly.






NoteGoing further: fitting the curve (optional)





fit_nlin() tries several standard curves and reports how well each fits. In the table, values closer to 1 in the CCC and r_squared columns mean a better fit.

fits <- fit_nlin(time = mildew$time, y = mildew$sev)
fits$Stats

                 CCC r_squared    RSE
Gompertz      0.9854    0.9716 0.0281
Logistic      0.9756    0.9553 0.0358
Exponential   0.9590    0.9297 0.0454
Monomolecular     NA        NA     NA

plot_fit(fits) + theme_minimal()

title: 2. How epidemics grow
section: One number for a whole epidemic
text:
One number for a whole epidemic
To compare epidemics, for example under two irrigation methods, it helps to sum up the whole curve in one number. The area under the disease progress curve (AUDPC) does that. A bigger area means more disease for longer.

AUDPC(time = mildew$time, y = mildew$sev, y_proportion = TRUE)

[1] 13.44233

title: 2. How epidemics grow
2. How epidemics grow
text:
What to take away

An epidemic grows like sources times targets, which produces the S-shaped curve.
Check every formula at \(t = 0\). It takes ten seconds and catches real errors.
Summarise a whole epidemic with one number, the AUDPC, so you can compare treatments.

The ideas in this lesson follow the open textbook R for Plant Disease Epidemiology by Emerson Del Ponte, which is the best next step if you want to go further.

title: 3. Checking your own results
text: This lesson is about the habit that matters most in science: checking a result before you believe it. We use two real examples, and the first one is the instructor’s own mistake.

title: 3. Checking your own results
section: Part 1: Do the varieties really differ?
text:
Part 1: Do the varieties really differ?
For a final-year thesis at Bells University of Technology, twenty traditional varieties of common bean from Kano were grown in a screen house. Each variety was grown in two pots, with plants measured at two readings. The thesis reported that the varieties differed in how tall they grew.
Here is the week-6 plant height data:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

beans <- read_csv("data/bean_week6.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(beans)

[1] 80



ggplot(beans, aes(x = reorder(accession, PH, median), y = PH)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#e8e0c8") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Plant height at week 6 (cm)",
       title = "Plant height of 20 bean varieties") +
  theme_minimal()








The boxes overlap a lot. Plants of the same variety differ from one another by about as much as the varieties differ from each other. If that is true, “variety A is taller than variety B” is not a safe claim.

Putting a number on it
Here is a simple check anyone can do. Compare two spreads:

how much plants of the same variety differ from each other, and
how much the averages of the different varieties differ.


by_variety <- beans |>
  group_by(accession) |>
  summarise(average = mean(PH, na.rm = TRUE), spread = sd(PH, na.rm = TRUE))

tibble(
  within_a_variety         = mean(by_variety$spread, na.rm = TRUE),
  between_variety_averages = sd(by_variety$average, na.rm = TRUE)
)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  within_a_variety between_variety_averages
             <dbl>                    <dbl>
1             110.                     55.2


(na.rm = TRUE tells R to skip the few plants with a missing measurement, instead of giving up.)
Plants of the same variety differ by about twice as much as the variety averages do. When the differences within groups are bigger than the differences between them, you cannot honestly say one variety is taller than another.






NoteGoing further: a mixed model (optional)





A mixed model splits the variation into its sources: the variety, the pot a plant grew in, and plant-to-plant differences. It gives the same answer more formally: only about 8% of the variation in height comes from the variety.

library(lme4)
model <- lmer(PH ~ factor(reading) + (1 | accession) + (1 | accession:pot), data = beans)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
vc |> transmute(source = grp, share_of_total = vcov / sum(vcov))

         source share_of_total
1 accession:pot      0.0000000
2     accession      0.0804882
3      Residual      0.9195118











ImportantThe honest response



The thesis claims about height differences between varieties had to be withdrawn. That is not a failure: finding it, correcting it and publishing the correction is exactly how science is supposed to work. The full reanalysis is open on GitHub.

title: 3. Checking your own results
section: Part 2: What a survey cannot see
text:
Part 2: What a survey cannot see
In Lesson 1 we counted diseased plants by their symptoms. But the WAVE researchers also took leaf samples back to the laboratory and tested them for the virus itself. That lets us ask: how many infected plants did the eye miss?

library(readxl)

lab <- read_excel("data/cassava_mosaic_survey.xlsx", sheet = "Lab") |>
  filter(Host == "Cassava", !is.na(Symptom)) |>
  mutate(showed_symptoms = Symptom == 1,
         virus_found     = Result != "Negative")

lab |> count(showed_symptoms, virus_found)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  showed_symptoms virus_found     n
  <lgl>           <lgl>       <int>
1 FALSE           FALSE         372
2 FALSE           TRUE          228
3 TRUE            FALSE          66
4 TRUE            TRUE          651


Now the key number: of the plants that really were infected, what share showed no symptoms at all?

lab |>
  filter(virus_found) |>
  summarise(infected = n(),
            no_symptoms = sum(!showed_symptoms),
            share_hidden = mean(!showed_symptoms))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  infected no_symptoms share_hidden
     <int>       <int>        <dbl>
1      879         228        0.259


About a quarter of infected plants looked healthy. A survey that relies on the eye will undercount the disease, and those hidden plants keep spreading it.






WarningCheck how the sample was chosen



The plants sent to the laboratory were not picked at random: plants with symptoms were collected more often. That means the true share of hidden infections is probably higher than this. Always ask how a sample was chosen before you trust a percentage.

title: 3. Checking your own results
text:
Five habits that catch mistakes

Keep the raw data untouched. Do every step in a script, so you can rerun it from the start.
Test with numbers you already know, like checking a formula at \(t = 0\).
Look before you average. A box plot shows overlap that a table of means hides.
Ask how the sample was chosen. It decides what a percentage can mean.
Share your data and code, so others can check you. GitHub is free.

title: 3. Checking your own results
text:
Your turn






NoteExercise



Do the same check for number of leaves (NL). Are the varieties any easier to tell apart?








TipAnswer






by_variety_nl <- beans |>
  group_by(accession) |>
  summarise(average = mean(NL, na.rm = TRUE), spread = sd(NL, na.rm = TRUE))

tibble(
  within_a_variety         = mean(by_variety_nl$spread, na.rm = TRUE),
  between_variety_averages = sd(by_variety_nl$average, na.rm = TRUE)
)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  within_a_variety between_variety_averages
             <dbl>                    <dbl>
1             39.7                     30.8


The spread within a variety is still bigger, so the same caution applies.

title: 3. Checking your own results
text:
What to take away

A difference between groups only means something if it is bigger than the variation within them.
What you can see is not always all there is: test, do not just look.
Checking and correcting your own work is a strength, and sharing it openly makes everyone’s science better.

title: Analysing Crop Disease Data in R
text:
Every season, Nigerian farmers lose crops to disease that was only noticed once it was too late to stop. Seeing an outbreak early starts with being able to read disease data properly, and that is a skill most of us were never taught.
This course teaches it in three short lessons, using real Nigerian data: a survey of cassava mosaic disease across 512 fields in 13 states, and a bean trial grown at Bells University of Technology.

title: Analysing Crop Disease Data in R
text:
Who it is for
Final-year and postgraduate students in plant science, agriculture, biotechnology and related fields. No programming experience is needed. If you can use a spreadsheet, you can follow along.

title: Analysing Crop Disease Data in R
text:
What you will learn



Lesson
Topic
You will be able to




1
Reading disease data
load a real field survey, measure how much disease there is, and find where it came from


2
How epidemics grow
describe and fit the S-shaped curve of an epidemic, and check a model with one simple test


3
Checking your own results
test whether a result is real before you report it, and share your work so others can check it

title: Analysing Crop Disease Data in R
text:
How it works

Self-paced. Work through the three lessons in order, whenever suits you. Each takes about 90 minutes.
Free, with nothing to install. You can run everything in your web browser, so you do not need a powerful laptop. See Get set up.
Learn by doing. Every lesson uses real data, and ends with exercises whose answers you can reveal when you are ready.

title: Analysing Crop Disease Data in R
text:
Questions and feedback
Stuck, or found a mistake? Open an issue on GitHub and describe what happened. Feedback on what worked and what did not helps make the course better for the next student.

title: Analysing Crop Disease Data in R
text:
Run by
Raphael Odera Onunkwor, a biotechnology graduate of Bells University of Technology (First Class Honours, 2025) and a software engineer. He has rebuilt published crop-disease analyses in open code, and his correction to an open plant-disease epidemiology textbook is credited in its second edition.
The data used here come from other researchers who made them openly available. See Data and credits.
